meta.title: Who really said "The day of combination is here to stay. Individualism has gone, never to return"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Rockefeller really said it — but not in 1880. Verified on p. 622 of Allan Nevins’s 1940 biography, quoting the 1917–1920 Inglis interviews.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The day of combination is here to stay. Individualism has gone, never to return'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Rockefeller, wrong date. We traced the exact wording to Nevins (1940), p. 622, sourced to William Inglis's 1917-1920 interviews.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1839–1937 · Founder of Standard Oil & pioneering philanthropist
answer.sourceLine: The wording is genuine. It appears verbatim on page 622 of volume one of Allan Nevins’s John D. Rockefeller: The Heroic Age of American Enterprise (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1940), where Nevins footnotes it to William O. Inglis’s unpublished Conversations with Rockefeller. Nevins presents it as a later-life reflection on the Standard Oil trust — not, as the quote sites have it, a remark from 1880.

source.heading: The source, traced

docMeta.dd: John D. Rockefeller: The Heroic Age of American Enterprise, vol. 1, p. 622
Allan Nevins · Charles Scribner’s Sons, New York, 1940 (two volumes)
William O. Inglis, “Conversations with Rockefeller” — interviews of 1917–1920, Rockefeller Archive Center
A late-life retrospect on the Standard Oil trust — not a statement made in 1880

source.excerpt: This movement was the origin of the whole system of modern economic administration. … It has revolutionized the way of doing business all over the world. The time was ripe for it. It had to come, though all we saw at the moment was the need to save ourselves from wasteful conditions. … The day of combination is here to stay. Individualism has gone, never to return.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced section with the citation “Allan Nevins, John D. Rockefeller (New York: Scribner, 1959), I:622” and the note “age 41, in 1880.” Quote Investigator has no article on this quote, so that entry is the only prior research to work from.

The page reference proved real. The full text of volume one of Nevins’s 1940 first edition ↗ contains the two sentences verbatim on page 622, in the chapter on the first great trust, attributed to Rockefeller.

Nevins’s footnote for the passage reads simply “Inglis, Conversations with Rockefeller.” That manuscript is the John D. Rockefeller interview, 1917–1920 ↗, conducted by William O. Inglis and issued on microfiche in 1984 by Meckler with the Rockefeller Archive Center.

The date and edition in circulation do not survive that check: Nevins frames the words as a later-life reflection, and the 1959 Scribner “John D. Rockefeller” ↗ is a one-volume abridgement with no volume I and no page 622.
source.excerptNote: In Nevins the first sentence is set off by a short narrative aside before the quotation resumes; the second ellipsis is Nevins’s own, marking words he omitted. The famous two sentences close the passage exactly as shown.

source.rightsNote: The words are Rockefeller’s, but their first publication was in Allan Nevins’s biography of 1940, which is well inside the US copyright term, and the Inglis transcripts they were taken from stayed unpublished until the Rockefeller Archive Center microfiche edition of 1984. Short quotation with attribution is ordinary fair use; the surrounding Nevins narrative is not free to reproduce, and this line should not be treated as public domain.

author.name: John D. Rockefeller
author.heading: About the speaker
author.metaLine: 1839–1937 · American oil magnate, founder of Standard Oil, philanthropist
author.bio: John Davison Rockefeller (8 July 1839 – 23 May 1937) built Standard Oil from an 1870 Ohio corporation into the combination that dominated American oil refining, and became the era’s defining symbol of industrial consolidation. He was famously reticent in public, which is why so much of what we have in his own voice comes from a handful of late-life sources: his 1909 memoir Random Reminiscences of Men and Events, and the long series of interviews he gave the journalist William O. Inglis between 1917 and 1920 for an authorised biography that was never finished. He spent his last decades giving the fortune away through the Rockefeller Foundation and its sibling institutions.

Rockefeller: The Heroic Age of American Enterprise, vol. 1 (Scribner, 1940), p. 622, from William O. Inglis's 1917–1920 interviews. Genuine wording; commonly misdated to 1880.

misattribution.heading: What everyone gets wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right; the framing is not. Almost every quote site presents these two sentences as a standalone pronouncement made in 1880, when Rockefeller was 41, and cites a 1959 Scribner edition of Nevins. Two of those three details fall apart on contact with the book.

items.why: This gloss travels with the quote across Wikiquote ↗ and its downstream copies such as LibQuotes ↗. But in Nevins’s text ↗ the passage is introduced as something Rockefeller believed “in later life,” and it is footnoted to the Inglis conversations, which were recorded between 1917 and 1920. The page it sits on discusses the trust of 1882 and the New Jersey holding-company law of 1889 — events still in the future in 1880.

The 1959 Scribner book is a one-volume abridgement of about four hundred pages ↗, so it has neither a volume I nor a page 622. The volume-and-page reference belongs to the two-volume first edition of 1940, where the sentences do appear exactly as quoted.

The two sentences are the tail of a longer answer about the Standard Oil combination, and the ellipsis immediately before them is Nevins’s own, marking material he cut. Circulated alone, the line reads as prophecy; in context ↗ it reads as self-defence.

misattribution.truthLine: Rockefeller did say it — to a journalist compiling an authorised life that never appeared, looking back on a trust he had built decades earlier — and the words first reached print in Allan Nevins’s biography of 1940 ↗, not in 1880.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Rockefeller signed the Standard Oil Trust agreement on 2 January 1882 ↗, pooling the securities of some forty companies under nine trustees. It was a legal invention as much as a commercial one, and within a decade sugar, whiskey and a crowd of other industries had copied the template. These two sentences are Rockefeller’s own verdict on that invention — delivered decades later, to a friendly journalist, with no trace of apology.

That is what makes the line interesting and what makes the popular misdating so misleading. Read as a boast from 1880, it sounds like a young magnate announcing the future. Read where it actually sits — in the 1917–1920 Inglis interviews ↗, given for a biography that was never published — it is an old man defending his life’s work against a generation of critics, insisting that combination was not a choice but a necessity.
detailsBody: Inglis’s transcripts ran to a large body of typescript that was never turned into the authorised biography it was commissioned for. The material sat unpublished until Nevins drew on it for his 1940 study; the transcripts themselves were only issued to researchers in 1984, on microfiche, by Meckler in association with the Rockefeller Archive Center, with an index compiled by David Freeman Hawke.

The line is not in Rockefeller’s own memoir. A full-text search of Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909) ↗ at Project Gutenberg returns no hit for “day of combination,” “here to stay” or even the word “individualism.” Anyone citing the memoir for this quote is citing the wrong book.
